issues.issue: The clause equates masculine terms with all employees, but the operative text elsewhere uses "men" as a substantive category (e.g. 4-A.3 "No man may hold a regular situation", Group 4 "Casuals—Men"). Whether this preamble merely neutralizes gendered wording or reaches those defined categories is unstated.
The Agreement is made binding on each Publisher "or its successor" without defining what constitutes a successor or what obligations pass. Nothing in the instrument supplies the test.

The Metropolitan Area is fixed by "a radius of approximately fifty miles" and a line "bounded approximately as follows," leaving the outer boundary indeterminate. Whole obligations turn on it (2-E.1, 3-E, 9-A, 21-D.V "territorial coverage").

Recognition is tied to an enumerated list of operations, inviting an expressio unius reading that unlisted delivery-room work is outside the unit. The "Collectors, except ... billing system operated through the auditing department" carve-out compounds which collections are covered.

The exception for "a hospital, club comprising one building, school or other government or municipal building" ends in a general term after specific examples, leaving unclear which premises get single drop-off treatment. "Current practice in the territory" for collections and returns is likewise unfixed.

Coverage of "any other operation" depends on work "now being performed exclusively" by unit employees, and neither "now" (as of which agreement) nor "exclusively" is defined. The catch-all sits against the closed list in 2-A.1.

"New mechanical devices ... introduced to perform or aid in the performance of" unit operations has no boundary — a device that merely aids may or may not fall within it. The line against automated systems governed by 3-D.4 is not drawn.

Only terminals "located within the City of New York" are recognized as delivery points, inviting the argument that terminals elsewhere in the Metropolitan Area are excluded. The provision does not say whether the list is exhaustive.

Canada points may be established for areas "where for any reason distribution is interrupted," a trigger with no duration, cause or verification requirement. Nothing says when the point must be discontinued.

The ban on substituting buses, ferries or airplanes for "existing means or methods of delivery" is immediately qualified by a proviso preserving the right "to make substitution for a bus or railroad now being used," and the two sentences pull against each other. "Existing" and "now" are also fixed to no stated date.

Drivers are to be selected by seniority "in accordance with Section 4-B," but 4-B governs the filling of vacant or newly created regular situations, not the assignment of tractor-trailer work. The cross-reference cannot be applied as written.
"A reasonable number of employees" must be given training, with no benchmark, ratio or mechanism for fixing the number. Nothing else in the article supplies one.

The Publisher's reserved right to "continue and expand" the volume of work handed to an over-the-road carrier at the city line is hard to square with the Publishers' letter "Clarification of Method and Extent," which acknowledges that the contract prohibits subcontracting of bargaining-unit deliveries. Which governs an expansion of carrier work is unresolved.

Transfer points must lie "within the Metropolitan Area," but 22-D Point Two (iii) and (iv) direct The Times to select transfer points 150 to 250 miles from Columbus Circle, far outside that area. The two cannot both be given effect without deciding how far 22-D displaces 2-E.2(e).

Through-driving to "Albany or any other city designated by the Publisher" conflicts with 22-D Point Two(i), which excepts common-carrier runs beyond 250 miles or with more than two stops from unit driving. Which controls a long designated run is unstated.
Combination runs turn on "presently recognized exchange points at or near the city line," a set never identified anywhere in the Agreement. There is no mechanism for fixing or changing them.

The Publishers may unilaterally discontinue runs on a "jurisdictional dispute with another union," which is difficult to reconcile with 16-M.3's rule that no change in condition may be put into effect without the other party's prior consent. Neither provision says which prevails.

The right to increase, decrease or discontinue over-the-road trucking "to the extent that such forms of transportation may now be employed" is expressly narrowed for The Times by 22-D Point Two(x), which forbids assigning to a common carrier a run in operation nine consecutive months. The scope of paragraph (h) therefore differs by Publisher without the text saying so.

The no-layoff protection applies only where the layoff is "solely as a result of" establishing the run, a causation word with no test, and 3-D.1 preserves layoffs for economic or business reasons generally. Which characterization applies to a layoff following a new trailer run is left open.

The requirement that home-delivery bundles be tied by unit employees is qualified by "present practice, however, excepted," an unidentified body of practice that may swallow the rule. Neither the practice nor its date is fixed.

The Union's obligation to arbitrate jurisdictional conflicts is conditioned on "such other union or unions agree[ing] to such an arbitration," so the duty may never mature and no alternative is provided. "Conditions and methods of operation now prevailing" is likewise undated.

Union jurisdiction attaches "when full operations commence" at an annex or new building, and "full operations" is nowhere defined or measured. Partial or phased start-ups fall outside any stated rule.

Protection turns on an employee "performing satisfactorily the particular work assigned to him," with no standard for satisfactory performance. 4-A.4's "qualified and competent" requirement uses a different formulation for the same subject.

The first sentence is mutilated — "Any employee shall be entitled to for work in the performance of the several operations set forth in this section of the office or plant" — omitting the verb (apparently "to shape") that carries the right. What entitlement is created cannot be read off the words.

The clause promises maximum union security "to the extent embodied in Section 17 of this agreement," but 17-A.1 states that the union-security language printed there is "for reference only and not as a part of this Agreement." The reference therefore points to text the contract disclaims.

The sixth-shift overtime sentence reproduces, nearly word for word, part of the italicized former "2-L" set out in 17-A.1 as not part of this Agreement. Two provisions bearing the same section designation, one operative and one disclaimed, cannot be read together without construction.

The flat bar on an employee engaging "any person to aid him in the performance of the work assigned to him" sits against Section 10-B, which defines a half-day boy as working "in aid of and under the direction of a route man." Whether the routeman's use of a half-day boy is excepted is not stated.

Deductions are fixed to "the second pay check of the employee in each month," while the October 26, 1981 Weekly Checkoff letter obliges the Publisher to amend 2-N.1 for weekly or bi-weekly checkoff on sixty days' notice. The two prescribe different mechanics for the same deduction.

The agency fee is "a flat amount payable for each shift worked" but capped so that "the amount payable per shift" not exceed 5% of monthly dues, mixing per-shift and monthly measures. Whether the cap is per shift or on the aggregate is not resolved by the words.

The Publisher must continue "the schedules shown in the last notice of such schedules to the Union," an unidentified document with no date or copy incorporated. Which notice controls is left to proof outside the instrument.

This leaves "the conditions under which tailmen are to be employed" to each Publisher's published schedule, while 21-C.3(g) and the 21-D schedules fix tailman thresholds for The News by number of loads. Which source governs tailman manning is not stated.

The Union's right of complaint turns on schedules being "unduly burdensome," and the Publisher's on "newspaper operational conditions warrant[ing]" a change; neither phrase has a defined content. Nothing in Section 16 supplies a standard.

The Publisher's right to fix "the number of dealers to be served on the several respective routes" cannot be squared with 21-D.I.A, which caps maximum dealers per route by papers per load at Newspoint. Which prevails on a News direct-delivery route is unaddressed.

The recognized right to lay off and rearrange routes "as such Publisher may find necessary or desirable" runs against 3-D.4, which forbids layoff of listed situation holders because of automation. Whether a rearrangement following an automated installation is reviewable as economic is the fault line.

The definition is circular — "economic or business reasons" mean "all reasons of an economic or business character" in their "usual and ordinary sense" — and expressly disclaims prior practice as a guide. It supplies no boundary for the term it defines.

The duty to "give employment to those regular situation holders laid off by the wholesaler or news company" cannot be squared with the hiring order and Adjustment Board lists of 4-A.2, which control who is hired and in what sequence. Where such transferees fit in the Groups is unstated.

The protected list is of situation holders "as of May 1, 1981" but the protection runs against automation installed "after May 1, 1965," a sixteen-year mismatch that the text never explains. Which date governs the protection is on the face of the clause unclear.

Everything turns on "a determination duly made" that automation created an excess of regular situations, yet the clause never says who makes it or by what procedure. The two-week deadline runs from an event no one is assigned to declare.

This preserves the Publisher's obligation under 5-G to maintain "as many regular situations as possible" while simultaneously subjecting it to 3-D.1's layoff right. The savings language leaves the two duties to be reconciled without a rule of priority.

Existing methods and extent of direct and combined delivery "are to be continued" with no change absent Board approval, while 3-F leaves the Publisher "free" to choose and change delivery form on new sections or routes. Whether a route is "new" therefore decides which regime applies, and neither provision defines it.
"New sections or new routes" is undefined, so a rearranged or combined existing route may be recast as new and taken out of 3-E's freeze. The clause supplies no test for novelty.

This paragraph is reproduced verbatim as 12-C in the wholesalers section, so the same subject is governed twice in different places. A court asked whether one qualifies or supersedes the other has nothing in the text to go on.

The safety duties are stated as "undue hardship or hazard," "excessive work tasks" and protection "insofar as practicable," none of which has a defined measure. The provision then routes non-compliance complaints to the Board without supplying a standard for it to apply.

The insurance amount reads "$20,000, $50,000 beginning January 1, 1982," leaving both the initial figure and the mechanics of the increase uncertain on the face of the clause. The 1987 Memorandum's reference to raising this coverage "from $60,000" does not match either printed number.

The parties must make "every effort" to eliminate advance-section overtime "in so far as that may be practicable," and the same sentence then disclaims any obligation to do so. The duty created is not measurable.

The Publisher may purchase employee-owned equipment "at its then fair value," with no valuation method or appraiser named. Termination of existing arrangements when equipment "no longer is fit for use" is equally unmeasured.

The first sentence lets advertising and promotional matter be "handled, distributed or disposed of as the Publisher may direct," while the second requires that a defined class of such matter "be tied, handled and delivered by an extra crew." The two directions conflict as to matter falling in both descriptions.

The most-favored-terms duty reaches contracts with "any person publishing within the City of New York," a narrower geography than the Metropolitan Area used throughout the Agreement. Publishers just outside the city line fall into a gap the clause never addresses.

The Union must use its "best efforts collectively and individually to promote the business and interests of the several Publishers," a duty with no benchmark and no stated content. Nothing in the Agreement says what performance satisfies it.

The enumerated "immediate family" includes "grandmother, grandfather" without saying whose — the employee's, the spouse's, or both — a point The Times had to clarify by side letter in 1988 precisely because the terms "have not always been interpreted and applied consistently." The list also mixes named relations with "legal dependents as defined by the Internal Revenue Code."

Foremen and assistant foremen are placed on the seniority and priority lists here, while 6-B makes their hours, wages and conditions "a matter of agreement between the Publisher and such foreman" with a right of removal at will. Whether a foreman carries seniority for layoff cannot be answered from either alone.

Seniority is given two meanings — length of service in the regular-situation capacity in (a) and "length of service based on regularity and continuity of service" in (b) — introduced only by the word "Otherwise." Which measure governs a given dispute is left to construction.

Group 1 listing may be approved for loss of a situation "because of illness, physical incapacity or for other such good and sufficient cause," a catch-all following two specific medical grounds. Whether the general words are confined to causes of that kind is the classic ejusdem generis question.

Group 3 status is given to "men who signify their intention to and do shape steadily," and "steadily" is defined nowhere. The shape requirements in 4-A.2(e) state a different, numeric test for retention.

Casuals are "men who are not connected with the industry," while "industry" is defined in 4-A.2(i) by reference to employing companies, not to individuals' connections. Who counts as unconnected is therefore untested.

Promotion to vacant regular situations is ordered from Group 1 then Group 3, omitting Group 2 industry extras entirely, while 4-B says such situations are "filled permanently ... from among the regular situation holders" by seniority. The temporary/permanent split leaves the two rules in tension.

Retention requires shaping six shifts "per week or work[ing] five (5) shifts per week," but credit is limited to one shift per twenty-four hours and only if present at hiring, so the two requirements may not both be satisfiable in a week. The interaction of the shape count and the credit rule is not worked out.

A foreman needing more men than the list holds "may engage such men as he may be able to obtain," which is difficult to square with the same paragraph's rule that only the Adjustment Board may add to or change the lists and with the hiring order of 4-A.2(b). The status of men so engaged is unaddressed.

The definition of "industry" is ungrammatical — "all companies employing persons engaged in the categories contained in Section 2 hereof by any Publisher, newspaper distributor or wholesaler" — so it is unclear whether the companies or the categories are being qualified. Group 2 seniority and Group 1 transfer rights turn on this word.

The 2% cap is measured against "the total number of situations in the delivery room of said Publisher," a unit of count that no provision defines for multi-plant publishers. 6-D contemplates more than one plant per Publisher.
The fractions are printed as "one third (4)" and "two thirds (34)," so the numerals contradict the words. The annual transfer allocation cannot be computed from the text as printed.

"Qualified and competent for the work or the job in question" states the hiring and promotion bar without any definition or objective measure of competence. 4-H sends such questions to the Board without supplying a standard.

The vacancy is to be filled permanently "from among the regular situation holders in accord with their seniority standing," while 4-A.1(b) says promotional priority — not seniority — determines who may claim a newly created or vacant regular situation. The two selection rules cannot both govern.

An unemployed (Group 1) extra who refuses a situation is "placed at the top of the Group 3 regular extra list" while a Group 3 extra who refuses goes to the end, so refusal moves the senior man into a junior group at a favorable position. Whether that is a penalty or a benefit is not resolvable from the words.

The exceptions apply only "provided notice in writing has been given to the Publisher," with no time limit stated for that notice and no consequence specified for late notice. Whether a belated writing preserves the situation is unaddressed.

Consent to a leave of absence "shall not be unreasonably withheld," a standard the Agreement nowhere elaborates, and the same test is applied again to extensions. There is no stated maximum duration for such leaves.

Paragraph (a) deems the situation vacated once the absence periods are reached, while (c) makes vacancy depend on a certified letter and the absence of an explanation within thirty days. Whether the situation is vacated automatically or only after the letter procedure is the conflict.

Restoration is given to employees "absent for the foregoing reasons," which may refer to the four enumerated reasons in 4-F.1(a) or to any absence covered by the whole of 4-F including (c). The antecedent is not fixed.

The day shift is defined as falling "between the period of 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m." while 5-B defines the night shift as between 6:00 p.m. and 10:00 a.m., so the two periods overlap by hours at both ends. Which rate and which shift rules govern work in the overlap is not stated.

The night-shift window of 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 a.m. overlaps the 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. day-shift window fixed by 5-A, and the Agreement pays different rates for each. Nothing designates which classification controls work performed in the overlapping hours.

The day work week is printed as "no more than 8915 hours per week," a figure that is not a number of hours and cannot be reconciled with the 7 hours 54 minutes day fixed by 5-A. The weekly ceiling cannot be read off the text.

The obligation to stagger the work week "so that as many regular situations as possible may be created and maintained" states a maximizing duty with no measure of what is possible. 3-D.6 makes this same undefined obligation the anchor of the automation protections.

Double time is required for Sunday advance-section work between 10:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., the identical window for which 5-K sets time and one-half for Sunday work. Whether advance-section work draws double time or the general Sunday rate is unresolved.

The Publisher may change a regular situation holder's starting time on four days' notice, while paragraph 4 of the June 23, 1981 Supplementary Agreement guarantees existing regular situation holders "against a change in their present starting times." The two cannot both operate for the guaranteed men.

Sunday work between 10:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. is paid at time and one-half here, but 5-I commands double the regular and overtime rates for advance-section work in exactly that window. The provisions overlap without a priority rule.

Compensation is owed where a job finishes "sufficiently far from where it began to involve substantial travel time," and neither the distance, the time nor the amount of compensation is fixed. The clause simply directs the parties to negotiate the arrangement.

A charge that overtime is "required or distributed unfairly" may be taken to the Board, but no distribution rule or standard of fairness appears anywhere. 8-C uses a different (discrimination) test for the same subject as to chapel chairmen.

The paid-lunch rule and its time-and-one-half penalty apply to inside employees, yet the Carlstadt minutes in 22-A fix different lunch and coffee-break entitlements for delivery-department floormen and truck loaders, and 21-D.IV fixes a 45-minute lunch at Newspoint. Which regime supplies the entitlement and the penalty at those plants is not stated.

Foremen's hours, wages and conditions are made a matter of individual agreement with a Publisher right of removal, while 4-A.1(a) places foremen on the seniority and priority lists that govern layoff. Whether the individual agreement can override the seniority list is unaddressed.

The duty to have a foreman "whenever a Publisher has more than one plant" leaves the single-plant case unstated, an omission the parties later cured by rewriting the sentence to "one or more plants." As printed the provision says nothing about the ordinary case.

Only the foreman or assistant-in-charge may "issue orders and make changes in operating procedures," which sits awkwardly with the Publishers' express rights elsewhere (e.g. 3-B, 3-D.1, 20-E.7) to direct and rearrange operations. The clause does not say whether it is merely a channel rule or a substantive limit.

A Publisher may complain that the Union "improperly imposed penalties" on a foreman, but neither this clause nor 6-A.2 says what makes an internal union penalty improper. The standard is left to the Board without content.

Entitlement runs to the listed holidays "or days observed as such," a phrase that is nowhere defined and could mean the employer's observance, the legal observance, or the industry's. The forfeiture rule for an employee who "trips" turns on the same undefined day.

The holiday runs "from the beginning of the night shift on the night before the holiday to the end of the day shift of the holiday itself," which leaves the night shift beginning on the holiday evening outside the holiday period. Whether that shift is paid at holiday rates cannot be answered from the words.

The premium is printed as "price and one-half of the holiday rate" and the sick-leave cross-reference is to "Section 18-B. 2," a section that does not exist (13-B.2 is intended). Both errors go to the amount and the exclusion the clause creates.

Work on a holiday for a non-issuing Publisher is paid "at double the regular and overtime rates," while 7-C fixes not less than two days' pay for the regular shift and time and one-half of the holiday rate thereafter for any employee required to work a holiday. The two pay formulas cover the same work.

Chapel chairmen are protected "provided these activities do not interfere with the performance of their duties," and the same sentence then excludes claim presentation from what counts as interference. What other activity crosses the line is left undefined.

The Publisher must produce overtime records "within forty-eight (48) hours, upon request" for the preceding fiscal week, yet the same paragraph limits production to three weeks before a written demand. Whether the 48-hour duty requires a written demand at all is unclear.

This makes bulk delivery to the Publisher's plant mandatory for outside-printed sections, while 9-B requires only that the Publisher "endeavor" to have that bulk delivery performed by unit employees and excuses it for increased cost or jurisdictional conflict. The relation between the mandatory routing and the qualified manning duty is unstated.

The duty is only to "endeavor," and it is defeated whenever performance would "involve the Publisher in increased cost or a jurisdictional conflict with some other union" — neither qualifier being measured or de minimis-limited. Any unit delivery costs something, so the exception may consume the obligation.

Half-day boys may be employed "upon such terms as may be agreed upon between such boys and the Publishers," which sits against 13-C's floor requiring routeman rates for work under a foreman and against 2-K's bar on non-covered persons performing Section 2 operations. Where half-day boy work stops and covered work begins is not drawn.

The cap is set by the number of half-day boys "now employed" and by routes on which none is employed "at this time," with no date fixed in a 1981 agreement carrying forward decades-old text. The baseline against which increases are measured cannot be identified from the instrument.

The prohibition covers "any assistance in the matter of deliveries or distribution" given "directly or indirectly," a formulation with no boundary as between ordinary industry dealings and prohibited aid. 11-B assumes the point will be controverted without supplying a test.

The distribution ban applies only "to the extent permitted by law," so the scope of the obligation depends on an unresolved legal question the clause itself flags. Whether a wholesaler is "willing to enter into" an agreement is also left untested.

A wholesaler delivering only one newspaper is "deemed an employee of the Publisher ... subject to all of the terms and conditions hereof, present practices excepted, however" — an unidentified exception attached to a deeming rule of great consequence. What the deeming does to wage, benefit and contribution obligations is not spelled out.

This paragraph repeats 3-G word for word, so present practices as to wholesalers' receipt of newspapers are governed by two separate provisions. Whether one is surplusage or has a different scope is not resolvable from the text.

The Publisher's secondary liability is triggered by the wholesaler's failure to pay "within 380 days of the actual layoff," a figure that cannot be the parties' intent (30 days) and cannot be squared with the 60-day notice condition that follows. The trigger date is therefore unreadable.
The condition requires that "the notice of layoffs is given" within 60 days without saying who must give it or to whom. Failure of the condition defeats the Publisher's liability entirely.

"Financial benefits" is defined to include "pension and welfare contribution" on leave days, vacation and pay in lieu of notice, whereas 13-H.1 and 13-I.1 measure contributions by shifts actually worked with a five-shift weekly cap. How contributions are computed on days not worked is not addressed.

The Publisher's liability is capped at "40 days vacation" per employee, while 13-B.4 forbids any employee receiving more than twenty days' vacation in a calendar year in any one office. The two ceilings are stated in the same currency without reconciliation.

Where more than one Publisher is involved "the liabilities shall be apportioned by the Publishers so involved," with no formula and no recourse if they do not agree. The employee's entitlement depends on an agreement the clause does not compel.

The Publishers need only "endeavor to have said successor make the payments," a duty of effort with no measure and no fallback if the successor refuses. The employees' entitlement in a merger of wholesalers is left unsecured.

The printed rate table is internally incomplete — the day overtime figure appears as "$' .026" and several night entries lack daily or weekly amounts — so the scale for the first contract year cannot be read from the clause. Contributions and premiums elsewhere are computed off these rates.

The $6.00 per week per employee "will be allocated to a fringe benefit" without saying which benefit, who allocates it, or on what terms it "may be converted ... into a percentage." Since the Welfare and Pension contributions in 13-H.1 and 13-I.1 are percentages of the rate, the conversion changes the contribution obligation by an unspecified amount.

The third-year table is garbled (e.g. "$13. B62", "Short: Ni ht 15.466 308. *"), leaving several scheduled rates unascertainable from the text. The rates drive contributions and premiums elsewhere in Section 13.

The adjustment is "the percentage increase in excess of 6% in the Index ... multiplied by the day scales," which literally multiplies a percentage by a wage figure and leaves the night and Saturday scales unmentioned even though the result is "added to the day scales." How the adjustment reaches the other scales and the listed fringes is not stated.

The Union may terminate the whole contract if a federal wage-control program should "prohibit, nullify or reduce any scheduled wage increase," with no requirement of materiality and no procedure for exercising the right. What counts as a program that reduces an increase is undefined.

The schedule is built on "More Than" / "Fewer Than" columns that leave the boundary values uncovered — an employee with exactly 20, 32 or 44 days worked falls in no band — and the last two rows (223–225 and 224 and up) overlap. The vacation entitlement for those counts cannot be computed.

The vacation schedule is to be "arranged at the convenience of the employer, but on the basis of seniority," while 20-D gives the Foreman "the option to schedule vacations at his discretion using seniority to determine the order." Which of employer convenience and seniority yields when they point different ways is unresolved.
"Present practices concerning the splitting of vacations shall be continued" identifies no practice, no plant and no date. The rule cannot be applied without extrinsic proof.

A holiday falling in a vacation is paid at "a day's pay at straight-time rates," while 7-C entitles a regular situation holder not required to work to "a full day's pay or a full night's pay" in accordance with his shift. The night-shift holiday within a vacation is therefore valued two ways.

This sets a routeman-rate floor for employees performing work "outside the operations set forth in Section 2" under a foreman, while 2-K forbids employees engaged in any other capacity from performing Section 2 operations at all. The category of covered-but-non-Section-2 work is created here and nowhere defined.

"All overtime shall be compensated at a rate of one and a half times the regular hourly rate," yet 5-H, 5-I and 7-E require double "the regular and overtime rates" for certain Sunday and holiday work. The word "all" cannot be given effect alongside the double-time provisions.

The over-scale formula preserves a ratio to "the regular rate established at the time immediately prior to the execution hereof," a baseline nowhere set out, and the printed sentence is mutilated ("engaged in the net of any of the operations ... foF isher"). The rate the clause guarantees cannot be computed from the text.

This lets the Publisher modify or abrogate over-scale arrangements "at any time," while 13-E.1 preserves excess rates as personal to the employee "so long as they continue employed at such operation." The two paragraphs give opposite answers on the same excess compensation.

A routeman collecting his own route "shall receive two (2) days' pay for such collection," without saying per week, per collection cycle or per route. The Publisher's option between a special crew and route collections turns on that unstated unit.

The complaint right runs to "excessive or repeated shortages" with no threshold, and the relief is capped at "one-half of one per cent of the total papers handled" without a period over which to measure. Neither the trigger nor the cap is computable as written.

The contribution is "6½% of each employee's rate per shift for each shift worked by each employee in the bargaining unit," capped at five shifts "in any payroll week in any one office" — leaving open whose shifts count, what "rate per shift" includes, and how the cap applies to an employee working for more than one office. The additional flat per-shift amount is imposed on a differently defined class again (non-regular, non-Group 1 or 2, non-qualifying Group 3).

The employer bears "any increase in the employee's contribution above 30¢ per week required by law for Statutory DBL benefits," without identifying the plan, the base contribution, or how the shifted cost is remitted. The relationship of this transfer to the percentage contribution in 13-H.1 is unstated.

Defining "employee" for this Fund to include "any individual whose retirement was recognized by the Trustees" cannot be squared with 13-H.1, which fixes contributions by percentage of rate "for each shift worked by each employee in the bargaining unit." A retiree works no shifts, so whether and how contributions attach to him is unanswerable from the two read together.

Payments are to be accepted from "other employers of individuals working under provisions substantially the same as those of this Agreement," a standard of sameness with no measure and no one designated to apply it. Whether such an employer becomes bound to the Fund's terms, and on what "basis" its payments must be made, is left open.

The obligation is "8% of each employee's pay rate per shift for each shift worked by each employee in the bargaining unit," capped at five shifts "in any payroll week in any one office for any one employee," without defining "pay rate per shift," which employees are in the unit for this purpose, or how the office-by-office cap operates. The delinquency sentence then extends liability to amounts "required to be paid under this or any previous collective bargaining agreement" without limit of time.

22-D Point Two(vi) gives tractor-trailer drivers who work 45 hours without a fifth shift "benefit credits as if they worked the fifth shift (vacation, sick days, pension and welfare, etc.)," which cannot be squared with this clause's measure of contributions by shifts actually worked. Whether a contribution is owed for a shift not worked is the conflict.

Payments from the Union and from non-signatory employers are permitted only "to the extent that the Trust Agreement may so provide," incorporating an external instrument whose Article 1 defines Employer and Covered Employee by reference to a collective bargaining agreement with the Union. Whether such payors become Contributing Employers under the Trust Agreement is not answered here.

Jury pay is owed for service "on a day when he normally would have been scheduled to work," a test that assumes a fixed schedule and gives no answer for a Group I extra who has none — the very gap the parties later filled by amendment in 1988. The clause fixes no way to determine the normal schedule.
The leave table uses "More Than" / "Fewer Than" bands that leave the boundary values (76, 118, 160, 202 days) in no band at all. An employee at those counts has no computable leave entitlement.

Accumulated leave is paid "at the then prevailing rate," while 20-A values unused paid leave at "his normal straight-time weekly pay" or, for partial use, "the rate he receives for the majority of his shifts." Two different measures govern payment for the same unused days.

Paid-leave days taken or cashed out are to be counted as days worked "for which welfare and pension contributions are made," whereas 13-H.1 and 13-I.1 tie contributions to "each shift worked" subject to a five-shift weekly cap. Whether a contribution is due on a day of paid leave is the conflict.

The Publisher's right is to discharge "for cause," while Section 15 gives a claim to an employee "discharged without just cause." The two provisions state the discharge standard differently for the same discharge.

The Publisher must "make every effort" to place a discharged incapacitated employee elsewhere, with no measure of sufficient effort and no remedy specified. The clause then modifies priority and seniority only "to that extent," itself indeterminate.
Discharge for "a bad driving record" is neither defined nor tied to any objective standard such as license status or accident count. The mitigation duty is again only to "make every effort."

This gives a grievance to an employee "discharged without just cause," whereas 14-A recognizes the Publisher's right to discharge "for cause" upon a stated reason. Which standard the Board applies is not settled by either clause.

The thirty-day limit runs from when the party "knew, or with reasonable diligence should have known," and is then relaxed for grievances "found to be continuing grievances" — a category the Agreement never defines. Whether a claim is continuing decides whether it is waived.

The fifth impartial member is drawn by random method from the 16-E.2 list, while 16-M.5 requires that in change-of-conditions grievances the Impartial Chairman selected under 16-M.1 constitute the fifth member. Whether a dispute is a change-of-conditions matter therefore determines which selection route applies, and nothing classifies it.

"No name may appear on more than one list" is ambiguous as between the AAA panels supplied for separate selections and the parties' own list of fifteen. The consequence of a duplicate name is not stated.

A quorum is "the chairman and any two other members," which permits a three-member panel drawn wholly from one side of the four partisan designees. The clause does not require balanced representation.

This speaks of "the permanent impartial chairmen designated under Section 16-M," but 16-M.1 provides for a chairman selected annually for each contract year, not a permanent one. The description does not match the office it refers to.

The Adjustment Board is given "exclusive jurisdiction over any issue arising with regard to the provisions of Section 4-A," while 4-H sends questions on qualifications, competency "or otherwise with respect to the interpretation or application of these provisions" to the Joint Standing Committee and/or Appeals Board. Two tribunals are given the same disputes.

The remedial power extends to safeguarding "the rights of the parties hereto or other person," an open reference to non-parties whose rights the Agreement nowhere identifies. The scope of awards in favour of such persons is undefined.

The annual selection procedure for the Impartial Chairman is displaced in practice by the October 26, 1981 side letter, which continues the incumbent "status quo" and alternate arbitrators until replacements are selected and have assumed office. Which instrument fixes the incumbent's term is left open.

"No change in condition shall be put in effect by either party ... without the prior consent of the other" leaves "change in condition" wholly undefined, and the exception refers to layoff "as hereinbefore provided in Section 8-D," a section that does not exist (3-D is meant). The parties themselves had to commission an arbitrator's written decision "interpreting the language of Section 16-M."

A change in effect more than thirty days "may be continued in effect pending a determination," which rewards the very unilateral action 16-M.3 forbids without prior consent. Which paragraph governs a long-standing unconsented change is unresolved.

This reserves change-of-conditions grievances to an Appeals Board chaired by the 16-M.1 Impartial Chairman, while 16-E.1 provides a random selection from the fifteen-name list for matters referred to the Appeals Board. Nothing tells the parties how to classify a grievance that mixes a change of conditions with its merits.

The no-strike duty is excepted "as against the party failing to comply with a decision, award or order," with no procedure for establishing non-compliance and no waiting period — conditions the parties later found it necessary to spell out. As written, self-help follows from a party's own assessment of compliance.

The italicized union-security text is declared "for reference only and not as a part of this Agreement," yet 17-A.2 makes that same text automatically part of the Agreement if it ceases to be barred by law. The clause disclaims what the next clause conditionally adopts.

The revival condition is printed as a provision that "no longer is held to be inoperative," a double negative that reverses the sense the parties must have intended. As written the trigger is unintelligible, and "the court of highest resource" compounds it.

A provision becomes inoperative on a conflict found by "any tribunal of competent authority," a body nowhere identified, and only "upon agreement by the parties" or an Appeals Board determination. Whether an outside ruling operates before the parties agree is unsettled.

Neither party may enter "any other agreement which in any way renders impossible or inoperative any provisions of this Agreement," yet 3-M expressly contemplates the Publisher and Union agreeing to differing wage rates and conditions for another publisher's plant. The blanket prohibition and the express permission overlap.

This closes bargaining on "wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment ... for the term of this Agreement," while the accompanying letters commit the parties to continued discussion of pension changes, Lancaster transport and the clerical-work study in 20-B. Whether those commitments survive the bargaining-settled clause is unaddressed.

Suspension and merger pay of eight weeks (40 shifts) is fixed here, while 12-D.1(3)(e) caps a Publisher's liability for the same species of benefit at "15 days suspension and merger pay" for wholesaler employees. The two entitlements are stated in different units and amounts without a bridge.

The Agreement is to "be treated by the Union and each such Publisher as an individual agreement between them," though the opening clause makes it an agreement by the Publishers' Association "as agent" binding on each Publisher. Whether joint or several obligations (e.g. the Association's undertakings in Section 16-O and the memoranda) arise is not settled.

The mediation trigger is printed as "a date thirty (36) days prior to the expiration date," the words and the numeral disagreeing. The date on which mediation may be invited cannot be fixed from the text.

Unused paid leave is paid at "his normal straight-time weekly pay" (or the rate for the majority of his shifts on partial use), whereas 13-K.2 pays accumulated and unused leave "at the then prevailing rate." The same days are valued by two different measures.

The parties agree only to a "joint study ... to define the types of clerical work which are appropriate to the deliverer's bargaining unit," leaving the jurisdictional question the study is to answer unresolved and unenforceable. No deadline, procedure or default rule is provided.

Group 3 and 4 men may not be assigned overtime "which would normally be assigned to employees who are paid a higher rate," and "normally" is fixed by no practice, period or plant. The prohibition cannot be applied without evidence outside the instrument.

A qualifying Group 1 man is said to be entitled to holiday pay "in accordance with Section 13-B. 4," but 13-B.4 sets a straight-time day's pay for a holiday in a vacation while 7-D fixes a full day's pay for qualifying extras. The cross-reference sends the reader to a provision that answers a different question.

The Memorandum operates "notwithstanding any provision to the contrary in the Agreement" without identifying which provisions it displaces, though Sections 3, 4, 5-J and 16-M all bear on layoff, bidding and changes in condition. The extent of the override is left to construction.

Protection from layoff is given but the holder "will be declared to be an 'excess situation holder' if his situation has been designated as an 'excess situation,'" a condition wholly within the Publisher's control under 20-E.4. Whether a man in an undesignated situation is protected is not answered.

The waiver excepts excess situation holders "who are seventy (70) or more years of age nor shall the provisions of Sections 3 and 4 of the Agreement be applicable to them," and the antecedent of "them" — all excess situation holders or only those aged seventy — cannot be fixed. On one reading the layoff and seniority regime is disapplied wholesale.

The News is bound to a 48-hour correction while "The Times will continue its present practice," an unidentified practice that fixes no obligation at all. The clause creates two different and one unascertainable standard for the same error.

The obligation is defined by sections "currently known as" Section 2 (Living) and Section 3 (Leisure) and by printing "on its own present press equipment," all fixed to an unstated date. Renaming or re-equipping defeats the description.

The limitation is expressed by reference to calendar quarters of 1974 and 1975, periods long past when this 1981-84 Agreement was made, yet the closing memorandum continues every memorandum and side agreement "through the term of this agreement and deemed updated." Whether and how these quarters are updated is unanswerable.

This states that the all-advertising sections agreement "ends effective March 30, 1975," while the closing memorandum provides that "every memorandum, letter agreement or side agreement shall be continued through the term of this agreement and deemed updated." A terminated agreement is reprinted as part of a contract that purports to continue everything of its kind.

The entitlement is fixed to four named individuals and triggered "when the regular roto is 75, 60, 50, 40 or fewer copies per load," a list whose terms are already "or fewer" and therefore redundant. Whether the benefit attaches to the jobs or the named men is unstated.

The guarantee of "no reduction in the present number of a.m. routes as a result of home delivery" is anchored to a stated count of 133 routes from an earlier memorandum. Whether the figure or the causal limitation controls a later reduction is not addressed.

The obligation is that the "Union to send letter that it will meet to resolve a problem of overtime ... if, under normal operation, one arises due to this paragraph." Neither "normal operation" nor the causal link to the paragraph is defined, and the promise is only to meet.

Tailmen are required above 180 loads "except as provided in the Newspoint Agreement," and the 21-D schedules set quite different load thresholds (up to 300 loads) for tailman use. Which threshold governs a given News run turns on the reach of that exception.
"Bindery Operation — Transport men hired according to need" states neither who judges need nor any manning floor. The entire obligation rests on an undefined standard.

The schedule column is headed "Maximum Number of Loads with 0 Tailmen" while the closing sentence states that "Tailmen will be employed on all runs covered by this Schedule 'A' except for recovery runs," so the table's premise and its text conflict. The rows are also out of order (45 papers appears between 100 and 50), leaving the bands uncertain.

The Suffolk schedule carries an asterisk after "Without a Tailman*" whose explanatory footnote appears only under Schedule C. Whether the "Schedule A will apply" fallback attaches to Schedule B is left to inference.

"Present practice with respect to running time will continue to apply" identifies no practice and no date, in a schedule that otherwise states precise numbers. Running time is left wholly to extrinsic proof.

"When pallet trucks are used present practice will be continued" fixes no load maximum at all, in contrast with the 250-load rule for non-pallet trucks in the preceding subparagraph. The governing practice is nowhere recorded.

Eight general floormen are "to be used when and where needed as directed," so the manning number is stated but its deployment is left entirely to direction. Whether the figure is a floor for hiring or merely an allocation is unclear.

Loaders "may be rotated with other delivery personnel" yet the specified numbers must be at the loading positions "whenever trucks are being loaded," and when positions are "down" they may be assigned only to floor work, mail runs or inter-plant deliveries. The permitted reassignments are an exclusive list that may not accommodate ordinary operation.

A worked lunch or coffee break at Newspoint is "compensated as provided in Section 5N," but 5-N compensates only a worked paid lunch at one-half hour of time and one-half and says nothing about coffee breaks or a 45-minute lunch. The cross-reference does not fit the entitlement it is applied to.

The obligation turns on delivery "within the contractually designated 'territorial coverage' of the Union," which Section 1 fixes only by an approximate fifty-mile radius and an approximate boundary line. Whether a given delivery point is inside or outside cannot be settled from the two provisions.

Delivery points outside the territory are to be designated by The News, with locations "in line with current policy" — a policy neither stated nor dated. The only constraint on the designation is thus unascertainable.

The 58 named men "will continue to be employed on the day side," and the next sentence says this "is not to be interpreted as a guaranty of 58 day jobs." The promise and its disclaimer occupy the same paragraph.

This declares that the Newspoint agreement "supersedes and replaces all other agreements, memoranda or practices" applicable to that operation, while the closing memorandum continues "every memorandum, letter agreement or side agreement" through the term. The two cannot both control a Newspoint side understanding.
"The IBM stipulation continues as it applies to the Daily News only" incorporates an outside document that is never described, dated or annexed. Its content cannot be determined from the Agreement.

This states that franchise delivery runs will carry papers "for the franchise dealers exclusively," repeating in different words the rule in 21-C.3(e) that home delivery runs will not service non-franchise dealers. Whether the two describe the same runs or different ones is unclear.
Lockers "will be reviewed and revised in a fair and equitable manner" — a duty with no standard, no deadline and no decision-maker. Nothing indicates what a fair revision would be.

The actuaries are to determine the funding cost "for the calendar year 1966," a date long past when this 1981-84 Agreement was executed, with no updating mechanism. The computation the paragraph commands cannot be performed prospectively.

The paragraph directs that "the Union shall select one option" with no time limit, no default and no statement of whether the 1970-vintage election has already been exercised. The Publisher's funding obligation in paragraph 1 depends on that unmade selection.

The comparability duty applies only where "it is mutually agreed" that another union's pension agreement grants improvements "which taken in their entirety, are more favorable," while the Publishers' October 7, 1981 parity letter promises whatever pension and welfare increases are granted any other labor organization without that agreement precondition. The two most-favoured-nation promises are stated on different terms.

The expiration sentence is broken off — "will expire in three years [from March $1," — leaving the terminal date unstated. Whether the zone-route arrangement runs to the contract's end cannot be read from the words.

The recital of Carlstadt's purpose commits both parties to "maximum productivity and efficiency ... consistent with the terms of this memorandum and of the contract" while preserving the Union's right to negotiate necessary manning. The aspirational passage can be argued either to inform or to yield to the specific jurisdiction and manning provisions that follow.

The paragraph as printed is spliced — a sentence granting the delivery department "exclusive jurisdiction of the Sta-Hi Newstrack and of all" is inserted into the middle of the sentence about placing color sections "prior to the start each week of mail room operations." Neither obligation can be read as a complete sentence.

Jurisdiction is over insert tying lines "destined for city delivery, or percentage equivalent of the city circulation which is approximately 4" — a figure with no unit that cannot be a percentage. The share of combo-run ITLs belonging to the delivery department is therefore unascertainable.

The delivery department has jurisdiction of press tying lines for papers destined for New York City "or percentage equivalent of city circulation," without saying who elects between the two measures or how the percentage is computed. The alternative may be given in place of the jurisdiction itself.

The Sta-Hi heading is followed only by the fragment "truck loaders, including, but not limited to, operations, control and clearing of jams," the granting words having been displaced into the earlier offloading paragraph. As printed the clause has no subject or verb.

After a list of named operations, jurisdiction is extended to "any operations over which the delivery department had jurisdiction at 43d Street, whether by contract or by precedent," an unbounded residual resting on unrecorded precedent. Whether the general words are confined to operations of the enumerated kind is the classic question.

The break entitlement is printed as "two 165-minute coffee breaks or one 80-minute coffee break," figures that cannot be right and are not equivalent to each other. The actual entitlement cannot be read from the text.

The obligations are pinned to runs "handled as of November 1, 1975" and to deadlines of 1977, all long past at the effective date of this 1981-84 Agreement. Whether anything remains to be performed under the paragraph is unstated.
The sentence breaks off at "provided that such other destination is at a location further" — further than what is never said. The condition on eliminating the Hightstown transfer point is incomplete.

The amendment operates on "the phrase '89 miles' as printed in the middle of Paragraph (ix) on Page 85 of the 1973-75 contract booklet," an external document, whereas the (ix) reprinted in this book already reads 27 miles. The instruction is either spent or self-referential.

"Combos and 5/3 sheets will be 'kicked off' in variables of five" uses trade shorthand that the Agreement nowhere defines, and "The Sunday completes will be continued to kick off as heretofore" points to an unrecorded practice. Neither obligation is ascertainable from the instrument.

The parties agree only to "observe the new conveyor system to determine manpower requirements," without saying who decides, by what standard, or what happens if they disagree. The manning consequence of the installation is left open.

These relief times (20 minutes per trailer, 15 per suburban or mail bag truck) duplicate the relief periods promised in the Carlstadt minutes under 22-A, which state them as a continuation of what "the office will continue to give." Whether the same relief is owed once or under two separate undertakings is unclear.

Relief disputes "will be brought to Theodore Kheel for decision," naming an individual rather than an office, while Section 16 routes disputes over interpretation and application of the Agreement to the Joint Standing Committee and Appeals Board. Nothing provides for Mr. Kheel's unavailability or for the overlap with Section 16.

The decisions "relate to the future; they are prospective," and 2-E.2 continues to apply to existing runs "until they are in force" — with no statement of when or how they come into force. The trigger for the whole interpretive memorandum is missing.

Section 2-E.2 applies fully "except as to such modifications as are described in this letter," though the document is headed as a memorandum of committee decisions and no letter is identified. Which writing carries the modifications is left uncertain.

The Times "will begin to apply the principle" that common-carrier over-the-road trucking will be done by covered employees, a duty of commencement with no completion date or pace. The exceptions turn on runs "now being done by common carrier," again fixed to no date.

Disagreement over the location of a transfer point is to be "considered a dispute under Section 16," whereas 2-E.2(e) provides that such a dispute "shall be presented to the Impartial Chairman for final and binding decision." Two different fora are given the same question.

Drivers who work 45 hours without a fifth shift receive "benefit credits as if they worked the fifth shift (vacation, sick days, pension and welfare, etc.)," which cannot be squared with 13-H.1 and 13-I.1 measuring contributions by shifts actually worked up to five per payroll week. Whether a contribution is owed for a shift not worked is unresolved.

The obligations are keyed to "By January 1, 1974" and to runs "presently delivered," dates and facts long superseded when this 1981-84 book was executed, and performance is excused if "legal action cannot resolve the problem." What survives of the paragraph, and who judges the legal impossibility, is unstated.

Run time is one hour per 27 miles "in a run direct from The Times to a single destination," and for multi-destination runs the clause says only that "allowance will be made." The allowance is neither quantified nor assigned to anyone to fix.

The opening words are mutilated — "Paragraph (h) will be construed clude this stipulation" — dropping the operative "to include." The manner in which paragraph (h) is qualified must be supplied by the reader.

The paragraph announces that as baggage work "drops off, the assignments of these men will be changed as follows" without stating any measure or trigger for the reduction in work. The changes in paragraphs 2 and 3 are made to depend on an event nobody is given power to declare.

The employee may decline the increase only by submitting a form "by the deadline date clearly stated on the form," a date the Agreement neither fixes nor constrains. The employee's right depends entirely on a term supplied unilaterally later.

The loading schedule reads "bundle weight of 87 to 46 pounds, five high," a range that is impossible as printed (37 is plainly meant) and that would in any event exceed the 46-pound maximum set by 3-A.1. The Saturday-night exception for "a reasonable number of bundles" is likewise unmeasured.

The reservation preserves The Times' right to seek damages "with respect to any future incident," a category left entirely undefined and untethered to any breach of this Agreement. Nothing limits it to conduct of the kind that produced the vacated judgment.

Monthly installments of $1,250 on a principal of $177,844 would run for well over a decade, while the contemporaneous News letter promises that "when the six payments referred to in the Memorandum have been made ... The News will not, under any circumstances, require additional payments." The installment schedule and the six-payment discharge cannot both be given effect.

The Union gets the benefit of "more favorable terms or treatment" accorded any other labor organization on an arbitration award or judicial decree, with no measure of comparison and no procedure for determining favorability. The clause then says the agreement "will be amended accordingly" without saying by whom.

Acceleration is triggered if the Union violates "the provisions against strikes and disruptions of orderly relationships with the New York News," a description that matches 16-N only in part and adds an undefined category of disruption. What conduct accelerates the balance is unclear.

Thirty days' notice is required before "any major change in its operations which has an impact on a significant number of its NMDU employees," with neither "major" nor "significant number" defined and only one illustrative example given. The notice duty also stands beside 16-M.3, which requires prior consent rather than notice for a change in condition.

This memorandum leaves the meaning of Section 16-M to a written arbitral decision to be rendered later, incorporating "the three points concerning changed conditions" from a 1971 award in a different union's arbitration. The operative content of 16-M.3 is thus supplied by documents outside the Agreement.

"Every memorandum, letter agreement or side agreement shall be continued through the term of this agreement and deemed updated" cannot be squared with the reprinted memoranda that state their own expiry (21-B.4 ending March 30, 1975; 21-G.3 expiring in three years) or with 21-D.VIII's supersession of all other Newspoint agreements. What "deemed updated" does to dated and terminated side agreements is unaddressed.

The utility man may be assigned to jobs "including but not limited to" three examples, yet the same paragraph makes clearing log jams work that "may only be performed by the utility man." The open-ended assignment power and the exclusive reservation pull in opposite directions.

The floor-hire floor of eighty-one excludes "the 'Alco Men' or people performing functions other than regular floor work on the daily product," a class defined by an undefined trade label. "Normal reduction in press utilization" is likewise unmeasured.

Regular situation holders are "guaranteed against a change in their present starting times," while 5-J expressly permits the Publisher to change a regular situation holder's reporting time on four days' notice. The guarantee and the reserved right cover the same men.
The route "shall be filed by in-shop bidding," plainly a mistranscription of "filled," and no bidding procedure is identified. Section 4-B's posting and bidding rules are not referred to.

The Publishers commit to a posting practice "including, but not limited to, starting times and days off and job functions," then add that "these practices do not limit either party's rights under the collective bargaining agreement." The disclaimer may negate the obligation the letter creates.

The parity promise on pension, welfare and insurance benefits is defeated where improvements are "granted in exchange for productivity improvements (as determined to the Union's reasonable satisfaction) or are diverted from the negotiated pattern package," two exceptions with no defined content and one committed to the Union's own satisfaction. Whether an increase is caught by the promise is unascertainable.

The existing arbitrators remain on the list until a new list is selected "in the manner provided by the parties' Agreement," while 16-E.2 requires selection "immediately after the execution of this Agreement" and 16-E.3 fixes annual striking dates. The letter holds open a list the Agreement directs to be constituted at once.

The Publisher agrees to amend 2-N.1 for weekly or bi-weekly checkoff on sixty days' notice, while 2-N.1 itself fixes deduction from the second pay check of each month and remittance within thirty days. Until the amendment is made, which schedule governs is unstated.

The letter promises only that The Times "is happy to continue our discussions and review" of the Union's pension proposals, creating no obligation to reach or implement anything. Against 17-D's statement that the parties have bargained and settled these subjects for the term, its status is unclear.

The Lancaster transport proposal is conditioned on "such transport did not involve the Times in increased costs," the same undefined qualifier used in 9-B, and the letter commits only to discussion "before the operation begins." Neither the cost test nor the outcome of the discussion is fixed.

The program is to be set up only "if a sufficient number of employees are interested," with no number stated and no one designated to decide sufficiency. "Another acceptable bank" is likewise unqualified as to whose acceptance is required.

This promises Bostrum seats and under-the-seat heaters only in "new trucks purchased for The News," while 3-H.1 requires that within thirty days of the effective date "all motor vehicles shall be equipped with heaters and defrosters" maintained in good working condition. The letter's narrower undertaking sits against the contract's general one.

The News undertakes to require no further payments once "the six payments referred to in the Memorandum have been made," whereas the Memorandum of Understanding provides for monthly $1,250 installments against a principal of $177,844. Six such payments would discharge a small fraction of the sum the Memorandum says the Union will pay.

The letter is printed out of order, with the stray line "Newspoint written agreements" preceding the body and the closing sentence broken off at "The News will abide by all." What the commitment covers beyond the 48-inch skid-height award cannot be read from the text.

A memorandum deleted from the prior agreement "shall be applicable" if "there be a problem in the future arising thereunder," reviving a document that the parties agreed to delete on a condition that is nowhere defined. What counts as such a problem, and who decides, is unstated.

The letter addresses "eligibility for the Medill Plan," a plan named nowhere else in the Agreement and apparently a mistranscription. The rules of eligibility are left to be posted unilaterally by the Benefit Department.

Deductions are for "a reasonable period of time designated by the employee" on an assignment "satisfactory to the Publisher," leaving both duration and form to undefined standards. Nothing says what makes an assignment satisfactory.

The acknowledgment that the Agreement "prohibits the subcontracting of bargaining unit deliveries except as it may exist pursuant to the contract" is circular and must be read against 3-E, 3-F and 2-E.2(d), which preserve combined delivery through wholesalers and expansion of work to over-the-road carriers. Which of those practices survives as permitted subcontracting is exactly what the letter leaves open.

The obligation to issue separate vacation checks arises only "when the planned DEC System is installed and operational," a condition with no date and wholly within The News' control. Whether the promise is enforceable before then is unaddressed.
The annual statement of pension-credited shifts is again conditioned on the DEC System being "installed and operational," with no deadline for that condition. The reporting duty may never mature.

The News undertakes to report "credited shifts for which contributions were not made," a category that presupposes shifts carrying pension credit without a contribution — something 13-I.1, which ties contributions to shifts worked up to five per week, does not define. What makes an uncontributed shift "credited" is unstated.
The thirty-day deadline for retroactive payments is excused "if delayed because of an emergency or Act of God," neither term being defined nor limited in duration. The excuse has no outer boundary.
The Company agreed only that it "would explore the purchase and use of dehumidifiers," an undertaking to consider rather than to act. No standard, timetable or outcome is fixed.

The promise is to provide "sixers" for Newspoint night men "in the same percentage as they are currently available" to the day shift, using an undefined trade term and an unfixed baseline date. The quantity owed cannot be determined.
